I use power to weight ratio to judge a vehicle's potential, but it's only potential. There are so many variables in play: gearing, transmission type, how power is generated, power curve, tires—it goes on endlessly.

As a rule of thumb, think of it this way: most factory vehicles, just ordinary cars, fall somewhere around a 20-23:1 power to weight ratio. That's 20-23 pounds per horsepower. That's kind of the mundane baseline. But there are other factors, like torque and gearing.

Generally, a manual transmission is better than a traditional automatic, and a traditional automatic is better than a continuously variable transmission. Also, some vehicles, like diesel engines and especially turbo diesels, make little power but a lot of torque. A diesel hatchback can be as fast as a sporty model from 0-45 mph, but then falls off because it doesn't have the horsepower numbers to keep up.

Then there is the actual weight to consider. A 6000-pound vehicle with a 10:1 power to weight ratio will accelerate very quickly, but it's still a heavy vehicle and may struggle in corners and under braking. In contrast, a 2300-pound car with a 17:1 ratio won't accelerate as quickly, but is significantly better at braking and cornering. This is one of the reasons certain lightweight sports cars are so popular.

Lastly, how power is generated matters. Take a baseline 300HP. Consider a classic muscle car, a modern performance sedan, and an older luxury vehicle. The naturally aspirated V8 will be very responsive and have a natural torque curve, making for good acceleration. The turbocharged engine will take longer to spool up and build power (less true with newer vehicles) and may lose boost with speed changes. The supercharged engine will be more similar to the naturally aspirated V8 with a linear torque curve but loses some initial power to parasitic loss.

All this information is great to have and learn more about, but in the end, the only reliable test of whether a vehicle does what you want it to do is to drive it and see. The only benchmark is the seat of your pants.

I hated my father when I was a kid, absolutely despised him, because he never made it easy. I wanted little to do with him and swore I would never be anything like him.

It wasn't until I became a father that I began to appreciate what that really meant. He taught me, forced me really, to hold myself to a higher standard. Taught me about self-respect, honor, discipline. Doing the right thing for its own sake, not for fear of reprisals, nor for what rewards there may be. He taught me how to be true to myself and to constantly seek to better myself.

He was an undereducated veteran, got his diploma in the military, barely, and supported his family with the strength of his back. He always worked more hours than he slept. But he still found time to attend classes whenever we could afford it and to consume books constantly. Never fiction, only historical or educational texts. In his fifties, this man could outwork anyone on site. He could fix anything, build anything, and debate anything. He taught me to turn wrenches, taught me how to lay beads, but also taught me critical thinking and the value of education and intelligence.

He passed away two Decembers ago. He turned 60, and about a week later was diagnosed with liver cancer. He spent the next six months fighting like hell and reassuring all of us that it was going to be okay. That he was proud of us all, loved us all, and that he had made peace with this world. He had bought my mother a home in the mountains like he had always promised to do. He had granddaughters like he always wanted, and they knew him and would remember him. So he was okay with whatever happened. When he died, it seemed like a relief for him, but we're all still standing around sort of shell-shocked.

I sort of laugh now whenever I think back to my angsty little rebel self when I was a kid and how much I hated my father. I was such a jerk, but my father knew what it was like and he never made it easy for me. I'm sure it would have been easier for him to just let me be the little brat I seemed so bent on being. But he didn't, and now whenever anyone tells me I'm so much like him, I couldn't be happier.
